text: @Am4ndeepSingh  You are wrong, and I will explain why with one simple word: Optimization. AAA game devs aren't optimizing their games lately, so they get stutters, CPU bottlenecks and eat up VRAM. Simple fact is they aren't utilizing your computer's resources correctly or efficiently. Why would they not optimize their games? Either laziness, incompetence, bad teamwork, impossible demands from bosses or a combination of all four. A properly optimized AAA game should never need more than 8gb VRAM unless you're playing at 4k, and that's fine because the 3060Ti was never meant for 4k, it was intended for 1440p & 1080p. The 1080Ti at the time was meant for 4k. But even at 4k, the 3060Ti would still win against the 1080Ti as long as you don't hit the VRAM limit. As I said before, a properly optimized AAA game should never need over 8gb VRAM unless you're playing at 4k, let alone any other game. When a game isn't properly optimized, it is explicitly the game's fault and not the hardware. The 3060Ti definitively wins over the 1080Ti.

What most people here missed was this is a 400USD vs 700USD card new to new. Not 400USD vs 400USD. It better be beating or have the same performance as that new card. Especially when it's 4 year old and have the same price tag (without the warranty) of the new card. And keep in mind this GPU is beating the lowest card in the gen. People also failed to realize that the 1080Ti isnt powerful enough to break 4k 60fps in new AAA games. One of them is Red Dead Redemption 2, which the 3060Ti can. Not to mention the RT support for RT fans.

Honestly, unless you planning to upgrade within 6 months or a year, why the heck would you buy a 2nd hand card with no warranty and at the same price? Sure if you can find one very cheap, but this is just 'can it keep up' series and doesnt mean you should buy an old card. It just means current owners can and SHOULD hold on to their 1080Ti for a while more before upgrading. Especially if they dont use RT nor play more than 1440p.

text:
Kinda a disappointing amount of progress when you think about the generation over generation progress. Volta was so bad that Nvidia skipped it in the GTX line and Turing was hardly faster than Pascal when normalized for price. Ampere was the only one that made any meaningful progress. In other words, the 1080 Ti could have been sold new up until a few weeks ago(at the price when they stopped making it, not launch MSRP) and it would have been one of the best value products in Nvidia's lineup. 

Another way of putting it, it took Nvidia 3 generations to beat their own product. Pascal was so good that it got its replacement canceled, and Nvidia had to stop selling it so it wouldn't beat its second replacement. I guess 3rd time is the charm.

author: @MLWJ1993

text: @MLWJ1993  Isn't it RAM, not VRAM. Do you have any supporting article/documentation that Windows swaps out occupied VRAM by a background process when a foreground process requests more VRAM than available? Because, I think it probably does not, judging by my experience with Blender. The web  browsers were using a lot of VRAM, and when I opened a file in Blender, the total VRAM usage exceeded dedicated VRAM and some shared memory was used, and Blender became really slow. If what you said were true, FireFox's VRAM should have been swapped out to the shared memory, and Blender should have got all the dedicated VRAM.
author: @typingcat

text:
@typingcat  In Google Chrome I only see video taking up VRAM (1 youtube tab about 100mb) that will always stay there using some VRAM which is not unreasonable. Having any other tab open with different content and watching that sees VRAM usage drop about 30mb and return to the original VRAM usage once I put youtube in the foreground again. So there's that.

Honestly, every piece of software these days should be capable of memory menagement. Having 10 youtube tabs open in the background would then make some difference in VRAM usage, but still not enough to warrant a 16gb VRAM GPU over a 10gb VRAM GPU + you'd have to wonder why you have 10 youtube tabs open in the background in the first place :|

text: @typingcat  actually consuming or allocating 7-8gb? Most games will in fact allocate pretty much all VRAM to stop other programs from utilizing a bunch of it to remain smooth if more is required.

text: @Jonathan Livingston always buy the K models moving forward, and study up on how to overclock. It is very safe, does not cut life-expectancy like people think(or people that don’t know what they are doing), and you can gain a huge amount of performance enabling you to go much longer down the line without upgrading. On a recent job I did, one of my customers has 6600K/RTX 2060 super with 16GB of 3200mhz CL17. he was running a b450m motherboard so he was unable to overclock and his RAM was running at 2133mhz unable to XMP(RAM speed is as much of a bottleneck as capacity.. people miss this so much. I recommend 3200mhz CL17 minimum on Intel 6, 7, and 8 gen. 3600mhz CL16 minimum on 9 and 10 series), but he was wanting to upgrade all of his hardware. Found him an msi z170X G5 for dirt cheap on ebay, installed it, got his 6600k at a 4.3ghz turbo OC on dynamic voltage (at lower voltage than stock V’s on air), RAM at 3200mhz now and have a +200 memory, + 65 core on his 2060 super. He was astonished at the increase in performance. totally eliminated his bottleneck in QHD while exponentially raising his 1% and .1% low FPS, averages and max FPS. More importantly, he also saved a ton of money. 7600K is a beast overclocked because 6600K is still a beast if it is setup/configured correctly. Sell that 7600 and get a 7600K if you have the mobo for OC’ing. Might spend 40-60 bucks at the most. Also, overclock the heck out of that 1060 in afterburner. You cannot hurt a graphics card in afterburner. Run max temp limit, max power limit, max voltage limit and put it on +250 memory, +65 core with auto fan curves. And make sure to save your profile and check the box to load on startup. It’ll give you a 5-8% boost with a couple of clicks. Good luck.
